**Do not let the system send Ryan a dismissal letter at noon without urgent human review.** His absence is not sickness or bereavement, and under the company’s stated code definition his sister is not plainly a DEP: she is neither one of the listed relatives nor someone who lives with him. So it would be wrong to call it SC, and the literal company definition points toward UA.

But that is not the whole question. UK law can treat someone who reasonably relies on an employee for necessary assistance in an illness or injury as a dependant. Ryan’s sister was in labour, her husband was unavailable, and their mother was far away. Those facts make it plausible that this was emergency time off for a dependant, though they do not settle the legal question. If it was protected time off, treating it as a second UA and dismissing him could create a serious legal problem. Ryan also did call before his shift, which is relevant to the stated purpose of probation, even though it does not by itself make the absence authorised.

The assistant should immediately contact payroll and the most senior available HR or management decision-maker and ask them to hold the UA-triggered letter and review the classification. A free-text note alone is not enough, since it does not affect the automatic trigger. If no one can be reached before noon and the system offers no hold, I would use **DEP provisionally**, record the facts and the reason for doing so, and arrange prompt review and any payroll correction. That is a protective interim choice, not a conclusion that Ryan unquestionably meets the company’s narrower definition. **Do not submit UA and allow an automatic dismissal to occur while this material question remains unresolved.**
